How do I set up Windows Server Backup?

Windows Server Backup is the built-in backup solution:

**Install**:
```powershell
Install-WindowsFeature Windows-Server-Backup
```

**Create a backup schedule** (GUI):
1. Open Windows Server Backup (`wbadmin.msc`).
2. Local Backup → Backup Schedule.
3. Choose: Full server (recommended) or Custom (specific volumes/folders).
4. Backup frequency: Once a day (default) or multiple times.
5. Destination: Dedicated hard disk (best), shared folder, or volume.

**Command line**:
```cmd
:: One-time backup to a network share
wbadmin start backup -backupTarget:\\BackupServer\Backups -include:C: -allCritical -quiet

:: System state backup (AD, registry, boot files)
wbadmin start systemstatebackup -backupTarget:E: -quiet

:: View backup history
wbadmin get versions

:: Restore a file
wbadmin start recovery -version:10/12/2026-06:00 -itemType:File -items:D:\Data\important.docx -recoverTarget:C:\Restored
```

**PowerShell**:
```powershell
# Create a backup policy
$policy = New-WBPolicy
$volume = Get-WBVolume -VolumePath C:
$target = New-WBBackupTarget -NetworkPath '\\BackupServer\Backups' -Credential (Get-Credential)
Add-WBVolume -Policy $policy -Volume $volume
Add-WBBackupTarget -Policy $policy -Target $target
Set-WBSchedule -Policy $policy -Schedule 02:00
Set-WBPolicy -Policy $policy
```

**Bare metal recovery**: Back up with `-allCritical` flag. To restore, boot from Windows Server installation media → Repair your computer → Troubleshoot → System Image Recovery.

**Limitations**: No deduplication, no tape support, no granular Exchange/SQL backup. For enterprise, use Veeam, Commvault, or Azure Backup.
How do I configure IPv6 in an enterprise network?

IPv6 adoption is growing — here's how to implement it alongside IPv4 (dual-stack).

**IPv6 basics:**
• 128-bit addresses: 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334
• Shortened: 2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:370:7334
• Link-local: fe80:: (auto-configured on every interface)
• No broadcast — uses multicast instead.
• No NAT needed (enough addresses for everything).

**Configure on Windows:**
```powershell
# Check IPv6 status
Get-NetIPAddress -AddressFamily IPv6

# Set static IPv6
New-NetIPAddress -InterfaceAlias 'Ethernet' -IPAddress '2001:db8:1::10' -PrefixLength 64 -DefaultGateway '2001:db8:1::1'

# Set IPv6 DNS
Set-DnsClientServerAddress -InterfaceAlias 'Ethernet' -ServerAddresses '2001:db8:1::1','2001:4860:4860::8888'

# Disable IPv6 (if needed for troubleshooting)
Disable-NetAdapterBinding -Name 'Ethernet' -ComponentID ms_tcpip6
```

**Configure on a Cisco router:**
```
ipv6 unicast-routing

interface GigabitEthernet0/0
  ipv6 address 2001:db8:1::1/64
  ipv6 enable
  ipv6 nd other-config-flag    # Tell clients to use DHCPv6 for DNS
```

**DHCPv6 (Windows Server):**
```powershell
Add-DhcpServerv6Scope -Prefix 2001:db8:1:: -Name 'IPv6 LAN'
Set-DhcpServerv6OptionValue -DnsServer 2001:db8:1::1 -DomainSearchList 'contoso.com'
```

**Dual-stack strategy:**
1. Enable IPv6 on core infrastructure (routers, switches, DNS, DHCP).
2. Ensure firewall supports IPv6 rules.
3. Test application compatibility.
4. Roll out to endpoints.
5. Keep IPv4 running in parallel — full transition takes years.
What is a subnet mask and how do I calculate subnets?

A subnet mask determines which part of an IP address is the network and which part is the host (device).

**Common subnet masks:**
- 255.255.255.0 (/24): 256 addresses, 254 usable hosts. Most common for small networks.
- 255.255.0.0 (/16): 65,536 addresses. Large networks.
- 255.255.255.128 (/25): 128 addresses, 126 usable hosts. Splits a /24 in half.
- 255.255.255.192 (/26): 64 addresses, 62 usable hosts.

**How it works:**
IP: 192.168.1.100, Mask: 255.255.255.0
- Network part: 192.168.1 (first three octets)
- Host part: .100 (last octet)
- Network address: 192.168.1.0
- Broadcast address: 192.168.1.255
- Usable range: 192.168.1.1 - 192.168.1.254

**Why subnetting matters:**
- Devices on different subnets can't talk directly — they need a router.
- If a computer has the wrong subnet mask, it won't reach devices it should.
- VPN clients often get a different subnet, which is why they can't reach some local resources.

**Quick troubleshooting:**
If two devices can't communicate, check `ipconfig` on both. They need the same network address (based on IP and subnet mask) or a router configured between their subnets.
What should IT support people know about APIs?

APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) are how software systems communicate:

**REST API basics**:
- Uses HTTP methods: GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE (remove).
- Returns data in JSON format.
- Has URLs called **endpoints** (e.g., `https://api.example.com/users`).
- Uses HTTP status codes: 200 (OK), 201 (Created), 400 (Bad Request), 401 (Unauthorized), 404 (Not Found), 500 (Server Error).

**Why IT support needs API knowledge**:
- Many tools have APIs (ServiceNow, Jira, Azure, AWS, Slack).
- Automate repetitive tasks (create users, update tickets, pull reports).
- Integrate systems together.
- Troubleshoot API-based services.

**Testing APIs with curl**:
```bash
# GET request
curl https://api.example.com/users

# GET with authentication
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN' https://api.example.com/users

# POST (create)
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name": "John", "email": "john@example.com"}'

# PUT (update)
curl -X PUT https://api.example.com/users/123 \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name": "John Updated"}'
```

**PowerShell**:
```powershell
# GET
$response = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri 'https://api.example.com/users' -Headers @{Authorization='Bearer TOKEN'}

# POST
$body = @{name='John'; email='john@example.com'} | ConvertTo-Json
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri 'https://api.example.com/users' -Method Post -Body $body -ContentType 'application/json'
```

**Tools**: Postman (GUI for testing APIs), curl (command line), PowerShell Invoke-RestMethod, Python requests library.

**Authentication methods**: API Key (simple, in header or query string), Bearer Token (OAuth2), Basic Auth (username:password, base64 encoded). Never share API keys or tokens — treat them like passwords.
A user says their computer is showing a 'Low Disk Space' warning on the C: drive. How do I free up space?

Free space on C: drive: 1) **Disk Cleanup** — search 'Disk Cleanup', select C:, check all boxes especially 'Windows Update Cleanup', 'Previous Windows installations' (can free 20GB+ after a major update), and 'Temporary files'. Click 'Clean up system files' for more options. 2) **Storage Sense** — Settings → System → Storage → turn on Storage Sense to automatically clean temp files. Click 'Configure Storage Sense' and 'Clean now'. 3) **Move or delete large files** — check Downloads folder (often full of forgotten files), Desktop, and Videos. Use WinDirStat or TreeSize to visualize what's using space. 4) **Uninstall unused programs** — Settings → Apps → sort by size. Remove apps you don't use. 5) **Clear browser caches** — Chrome, Edge, and Firefox can cache gigabytes. In Chrome: Settings → Privacy → Clear browsing data → Cached images and files. 6) **Move OneDrive files to cloud-only** — right-click OneDrive folder → Settings → choose 'Files On-Demand'. Then right-click large folders → 'Free up space' — files remain accessible but don't use local storage. 7) **Reduce the recycle bin size** — right-click Recycle Bin → Properties → set to 5% of disk instead of the default. 8) **Hibernate file** — if not needed, disable with 'powercfg -h off' (saves several GB).
What are database backups best practices and what types of backups should I implement?

Implement multiple backup types: Full Backups capture the entire database—run weekly for most systems, daily for critical ones. They're the baseline for restoration. Differential Backups capture changes since the last full backup—run daily. Faster than full backups and restore requires only full + latest differential. Transaction Log Backups (SQL Server) or WAL archiving (PostgreSQL) capture every transaction since the last log backup—run every 15-30 minutes for critical systems. Enables point-in-time recovery (PITR). Best practices: 1) Follow the 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 offsite. 2) Encrypt backups, especially offsite ones. 3) Test restores regularly—monthly at minimum. An untested backup isn't a backup. 4) Document RTO (Recovery Time Objective) and RPO (Recovery Point Objective)—these determine backup frequency. 5) Monitor backup jobs—alert on failures immediately. 6) Retain backups per policy: daily for 7 days, weekly for 4 weeks, monthly for 12 months (adjust per compliance). 7) Use native tools (pg_dump, mysqldump, SQL Server Backup) or enterprise solutions (Veeam, CommVault). 8) Consider cloud-native solutions: AWS RDS automated backups, Azure SQL automated backups.
How do I configure a VLAN on a Cisco switch?

Basic VLAN configuration on a Cisco IOS switch:

**Create a VLAN**:
```
enable
configure terminal
vlan 10
  name SALES
vlan 20
  name ENGINEERING
exit
```

**Assign an access port** (connects to a PC/device):
```
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
  switchport mode access
  switchport access vlan 10
  no shutdown
```

**Configure a trunk port** (connects to another switch or router):
```
interface GigabitEthernet0/24
  switchport mode trunk
  switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30
  switchport trunk native vlan 99
  no shutdown
```

**Verify**:
```
show vlan brief              ! List all VLANs and port assignments
show interfaces trunk        ! Show trunk port details
show interfaces switchport   ! Detailed port mode info
```

**Inter-VLAN routing** (Router-on-a-Stick):
On the router connected to the trunk port:
```
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.10
  encapsulation dot1Q 10
  ip address 10.0.10.1 255.255.255.0
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
  encapsulation dot1Q 20
  ip address 10.0.20.1 255.255.255.0
```

Or use a **Layer 3 switch** with SVI (Switch Virtual Interface):
```
interface vlan 10
  ip address 10.0.10.1 255.255.255.0
  no shutdown
ip routing
```
What are the best practices for providing remote support to end users?

Effective remote support requires good communication and tools: 1) **Before connecting** — ask the user to save their work and describe the issue. Confirm you have permission to remote in. 2) **Use the right tool** — for quick sessions: Quick Assist (built into Windows), for enterprise: tools like SCCM Remote Control, TeamViewer, or AnyDesk. For command-line: PowerShell Remoting or SSH. 3) **During the session** — narrate what you're doing ('I'm going to open Settings now'). This builds trust and educates the user. Don't silently take control. 4) **Minimize disruption** — avoid reboots during business hours unless necessary. If a reboot is needed, give the user time to save work. 5) **Security** — never ask for passwords over the phone. Use the remote tool's secure credential prompts. End the session explicitly and confirm the user sees the disconnect. 6) **After the session** — summarize what you did and the resolution. Update the ticket. If it requires a follow-up (reboot later, monitor for recurrence), set a reminder. 7) **If the issue requires physical access**, clearly communicate that and schedule an on-site visit.
How do I write a Dockerfile and build an image?

A Dockerfile defines how to build a container image.

Example for a Python app:
```dockerfile
# Use official base image
FROM python:3.11-slim

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy requirements first (for caching)
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy application code
COPY . .

# Expose port
EXPOSE 8000

# Run the app
CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
```

Build and run:
```bash
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name myapp myapp:1.0
```

Best practices:
• Use slim/alpine base images for smaller size.
• Multi-stage builds for compiled languages.
• Copy requirements before code (layer caching).
• Don't run as root — use `USER nonroot`.
• Use .dockerignore to exclude .git, node_modules, etc.
What is the purpose of a certificate authority (CA) and how does SSL/TLS certificate validation work?

A Certificate Authority (CA) is a trusted organization that issues digital certificates, verifying the identity of websites and organizations. The SSL/TLS validation process works through a chain of trust: Root CAs are pre-installed in operating systems and browsers (like DigiCert, Let's Encrypt, GlobalSign). Root CAs sign intermediate CA certificates, which in turn sign end-entity (server) certificates — this is the certificate chain. When you visit an HTTPS site: your browser receives the server's certificate, checks the certificate chain up to a trusted root CA, verifies the certificate hasn't expired, checks the domain name matches, and checks Certificate Revocation Lists (CRL) or uses OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) to ensure the certificate hasn't been revoked. Certificate types by validation level: Domain Validation (DV) — verifies domain ownership only, quick and automated (Let's Encrypt); Organization Validation (OV) — verifies organization identity; Extended Validation (EV) — rigorous verification of legal entity. For internal enterprise use, you can run your own CA using Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) or tools like step-ca or CFSSL. Internal CAs issue certificates for intranet sites, code signing, Wi-Fi authentication (802.1X), and VPN authentication. Distribute the root CA certificate to clients via GPO or MDM.
Windows Explorer keeps crashing when I open a folder.

Explorer crashes are often caused by corrupted shell extensions or thumbnails. Try these steps:

1. **Clear thumbnail cache**: Run `cleanmgr`, check Thumbnails, and click OK.
2. **Disable Preview Pane**: In Explorer, click View → Preview pane to toggle it off.
3. **Check shell extensions**: Download ShellExView (from NirSoft), sort by company name, and disable non-Microsoft extensions one by one to find the culprit.
4. **Run SFC**: Open an elevated Command Prompt and run `sfc /scannow` to repair system files.
5. **Reset Explorer**: `Get-AppxPackage Microsoft.WindowsFileExplorer | Reset-AppxPackage` (Windows 11).

If the crash only happens in a specific folder, the issue is likely a corrupt file or thumbnail in that directory.
What's the best way to document an IT infrastructure environment?

Good documentation saves hours during outages and onboarding. Here's what to document and how:

**Essential documents**:
1. **Network diagram** – physical and logical topology. Include IP ranges, VLANs, firewall zones, WAN links, and key devices. Tools: draw.io, Lucidchart, Visio, NetBox.
2. **Server inventory** – hostname, IP, OS, role/purpose, specs (CPU/RAM/disk), location (rack/VM host), owner, and SLA. A CMDB (Configuration Management Database) formalizes this.
3. **Service dependency map** – which services depend on which servers, databases, and external APIs. Critical for impact analysis during outages.
4. **Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs)** – step-by-step guides for routine tasks: user onboarding, backup restoration, server patching, VPN setup.
5. **Disaster Recovery / Business Continuity Plan** – recovery procedures, RTOs/RPOs, contact lists, vendor escalation paths.
6. **Password and credential management** – use a secrets manager (1Password, CyberArk, HashiCorp Vault), not a spreadsheet. Document which accounts exist and who owns them, not the passwords themselves.
7. **Change log** – what changed, when, why, and who approved it.

**Documentation best practices**:
- **Keep it where people look** – a wiki (Confluence, SharePoint, Notion) that's searchable, not files buried in a shared drive.
- **Review quarterly** – assign owners to each document. Stale docs are worse than no docs.
- **Automate where possible** – use scripts to generate server inventories, network maps, and config snapshots.
- **Write for your replacement** – assume the reader knows the technology but not your environment.
- **Include 'last tested' dates** – especially for DR procedures.
- **Version control** – use git for infrastructure-as-code docs, or wiki revision history for others.
I'm getting 'Your disk is almost full' on my Mac. What's using all the space?

macOS doesn't always make it obvious what's eating your storage. Here's how to find out:

1. Check the built-in storage breakdown: Apple menu > About This Mac > Storage (or System Settings > General > Storage). This shows categories like Apps, Documents, System Data, etc.

2. Find large files: Open Finder, press Cmd+F. Change 'Kind' to 'File Size' and set 'is greater than 1 GB'. This shows your biggest files. Old VM images, Xcode caches, and video files are common culprits.

3. Empty the Trash: Right-click the Trash icon in the Dock > Empty Trash. Deleted files still take up space until you empty it.

4. Clear system caches: Open Finder, press Cmd+Shift+G and go to ~/Library/Caches. You can safely delete the contents of folders here (not the folders themselves). Same for /Library/Caches.

5. Check for Time Machine local snapshots: If you use Time Machine, local snapshots can take up a lot of space. Run in Terminal: `tmutil listlocalsnapshots /` to see them. macOS usually manages these automatically, but you can delete old ones with `tmutil deletelocalsnapshots <date>`.

6. Check for large app data: Some apps store huge caches. Look in ~/Library/Application Support/ for apps you no longer use.
Windows Update is stuck or failing.

Windows Update failures are common. Work through these fixes:

1. **Run the troubleshooter**: Settings → Update & Security → Troubleshoot → Additional troubleshooters → Windows Update.
2. **Clear the update cache**:
   ```cmd
   net stop wuauserv
   net stop bits
   ren C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution SoftwareDistribution.old
   net start wuauserv
   net start bits
   ```
3. **Run DISM and SFC**:
   ```cmd
   DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
   sfc /scannow
   ```
4. **Check disk space**: Ensure at least 10 GB free on C: drive.
5. **Manually download the update**: Go to Microsoft Update Catalog (catalog.update.microsoft.com), search for the KB number, and download/install manually.
6. **Reset Windows Update components** (comprehensive script):
   ```cmd
   net stop wuauserv
   net stop cryptSvc
   net stop bits
   net stop msiserver
   ren C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution SoftwareDistribution.old
   ren C:\Windows\System32\catroot2 catroot2.old
   net start wuauserv
   net start cryptSvc
   net start bits
   net start msiserver
   ```
7. **Check for metered connection**: Settings → Network → your connection → make sure 'Metered connection' is OFF.
8. **Group Policy blocking**: Run `gpresult /h report.html` and check for Windows Update policies.
9. **Error codes**: Google the specific error code (e.g., 0x800f0922, 0x80073712) for targeted fixes.
How do I set up Microsoft Intune for device management?

Microsoft Intune is a cloud MDM/MAM solution in the Microsoft Endpoint Manager suite.

1. **Enroll devices**: Go to Endpoint Manager admin center → Devices → Enrollment.
   - Windows: enable auto-enrollment via Azure AD Join or GPO.
   - iOS/Android: set up Apple MDM push certificate or Android Enterprise.
2. **Compliance policies**: define requirements — encryption on, OS version minimum, password complexity.
3. **Configuration profiles**: push Wi-Fi settings, VPN, email profiles, certificates.
4. **App deployment**: add apps → assign to groups → Intune pushes them to enrolled devices.
5. **Conditional Access**: integrate with Azure AD — block non-compliant devices from M365.

Intune replaces on-prem SCCM for cloud-managed endpoints and is included in Microsoft 365 Business Premium and E3/E5 licenses.
How do I set up a cron job to run a script automatically on Linux?

Cron is Linux's built-in task scheduler. It runs scripts at specified times.

**Edit your cron jobs:**
```bash
crontab -e
```

**Cron format:**
```
# minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week command
# (0-59) (0-23) (1-31)       (1-12) (0-6, 0=Sunday)
```

**Examples:**
```bash
# Run every day at 2:30 AM
30 2 * * * /home/user/scripts/backup.sh

# Run every Monday at 8 AM
0 8 * * 1 /home/user/scripts/report.sh

# Run every 15 minutes
*/15 * * * * /home/user/scripts/check.sh

# Run on the 1st of every month at midnight
0 0 1 * * /home/user/scripts/monthly.sh

# Run every weekday at 5 PM
0 17 * * 1-5 /home/user/scripts/daily-report.sh
```

**Important tips:**
- Use full paths for everything (commands and files). Cron doesn't use your shell's PATH.
- Redirect output to a log: `0 2 * * * /scripts/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1`
- Make sure your script is executable: `chmod +x /home/user/scripts/backup.sh`
- View existing cron jobs: `crontab -l`
- Edit root's cron: `sudo crontab -e`

**Troubleshooting:**
If a cron job isn't running, check `/var/log/syslog` or `/var/log/cron` for errors.
What is MTU and how do I troubleshoot MTU issues?

MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) is the largest packet size (in bytes) a network interface can send:

**Default MTU**: 1500 bytes for Ethernet.

**Why MTU matters**:
- Packets larger than MTU are either **fragmented** (split into smaller packets) or **dropped** if Don't Fragment (DF) flag is set.
- Fragmentation causes performance issues and can cause connectivity problems.
- VPNs, tunnels, and PPPoE add overhead, reducing the effective MTU.

**Common MTU sizes**:
- Ethernet: 1500
- PPPoE (DSL): 1492
- VPN (IPsec): 1400-1436 (varies by encryption)
- GRE tunnel: 1476
- Jumbo frames: 9000 (data center, NFS, iSCSI)

**Symptoms of MTU issues**:
- Can ping a site but can't load web pages.
- VPN connected but certain sites won't load.
- Large file transfers fail but small ones work.
- SSH works but SCP/SFTP stalls.

**Diagnose**:
```cmd
:: Windows - find the largest packet that doesn't fragment
ping google.com -f -l 1472  :: Start with 1472 (1500 - 28 byte header)
:: Reduce size until it works
ping google.com -f -l 1400
```
```bash
# Linux
ping -M do -s 1472 google.com
```

**Fix**:
```cmd
:: Windows - set MTU
netsh interface ipv4 set subinterface "Ethernet" mtu=1400 store=persistent
```
```bash
# Linux - temporary
ip link set dev eth0 mtu 1400
# Linux - permanent (in network config)
```

**Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD)**: Automatically finds the optimal MTU. Requires ICMP to be allowed. If your firewall blocks ICMP, PMTUD breaks, causing MTU-related issues. Allow ICMP type 3 code 4 (Destination Unreachable, Fragmentation Needed).
How do I configure a Linux server as a DHCP server using ISC DHCP?

Install: 'apt install isc-dhcp-server' (Debian/Ubuntu) or 'yum install dhcp-server' (RHEL/CentOS). Configure /etc/dhcp/dhcpd.conf: 'authoritative; default-lease-time 600; max-lease-time 7200; subnet 192.168.1.0 netmask 255.255.255.0 { range 192.168.1.100 192.168.1.200; option routers 192.168.1.1; option domain-name-servers 8.8.8.8, 8.8.4.4; option domain-name "company.local"; }'. For static reservations (important for servers/printers): 'host printer1 { hardware ethernet AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF; fixed-address 192.168.1.50; }'. Set the listening interface in /etc/default/isc-dhcp-server: 'INTERFACESv4="eth0"'. Start and enable: 'systemctl enable --now isc-dhcp-server'. Monitor leases: 'cat /var/lib/dhcp/dhcpd.leases'. Troubleshooting: check 'journalctl -u isc-dhcp-server' for errors. Ensure no other DHCP server is on the subnet (rogue DHCP causes havoc). Use 'dhcping' to test from a client.
How do I test a disaster recovery plan?

Testing should be regular and progressively more thorough: 1) **Tabletop Exercise** (quarterly) — gather the team and walk through a scenario ('The main file server failed at 2 AM. Walk me through your response.'). Discuss who does what, in what order, with what tools. Identify gaps in the plan. 2) **Component Test** (monthly) — test individual elements: restore a single file from backup, fail over a single service, verify backup integrity with checksums. 3) **Simulation/Parallel Test** (semi-annually) — restore systems to alternate hardware or cloud environment WITHOUT disrupting production. Verify that restored systems work correctly, data is complete, and applications function. 4) **Full Interruption Test** (annually, if possible) — actually fail over to the DR site and run production from there. This is the most thorough but riskiest test. 5) **After each test**: Document what worked, what failed, how long recovery took vs. RTO, and update the DR plan accordingly. 6) **Key metrics to validate**: RTO (did we recover within the target?), RPO (did we lose more data than acceptable?), and completeness (were all critical systems restored?).
How do I manage Terraform state and workspaces?

Terraform state tracks what resources exist and their current configuration.

**Remote state** (recommended for teams):
```hcl
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "my-terraform-state"
    key            = "prod/terraform.tfstate"
    region         = "us-east-1"
    dynamodb_table = "terraform-locks"   # State locking
    encrypt        = true
  }
}
```

**State commands:**
```bash
terraform state list                        # List tracked resources
terraform state show aws_instance.web       # Show details
terraform state mv aws_instance.old aws_instance.new  # Rename
terraform state rm aws_instance.web         # Remove from tracking (doesn't delete)
terraform import aws_instance.web i-12345   # Import existing resource
```

**Workspaces** — manage multiple environments:
```bash
terraform workspace new staging
terraform workspace new production
terraform workspace select staging
terraform workspace list
```

Use `terraform.workspace` in configs to vary settings per environment.
A user reports they can't access a shared network folder. What's my troubleshooting process?

Structured approach: 1) Verify the issue: can the user access ANY network shares, or just this specific one? If all shares are inaccessible, it's likely a network/authentication issue. If only one share, it's permissions. 2) Network connectivity: 'ping fileserver', 'Test-NetConnection fileserver -Port 445'. If ping fails, check: network cable, Wi-Fi connection, DNS resolution ('nslookup fileserver'). 3) Authentication: is the user's AD account locked? ('Get-ADUser username -Properties LockedOut'). Is their password expired? Can they access other domain resources? 4) Share-level check: from another machine, verify the share exists: 'net view \\fileserver'. 5) Permissions (two layers must both allow access): Share permissions (right-click folder → Properties → Sharing tab → Advanced Sharing → Permissions). NTFS permissions (Security tab). The effective access is the MOST RESTRICTIVE combination. 6) Credential cache: 'net use' to check existing connections. 'net use \\fileserver /delete' to clear stale connections. Check Credential Manager for saved credentials that might be wrong. 7) Group membership: verify the user is in the correct security group: 'Get-ADPrincipalGroupMembership username'. Group changes require logoff/logon to take effect (new Kerberos ticket). 8) Check for 'Access Based Enumeration'—the share might be visible but files/folders are hidden based on permissions.
My monitor resolution is wrong and I can't change it.

If your display is stuck at a low resolution:

1. **Install the GPU driver**: A missing or generic driver is the #1 cause. Download from NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel.
2. **Check cable bandwidth**: VGA tops out at 1920x1200. For 4K, you need HDMI 2.0+ or DisplayPort 1.2+.
3. **Install monitor driver/ICC profile**: Some monitors need their own driver. Check the manufacturer's website.
4. **Use GPU control panel**: NVIDIA Control Panel → Change resolution, or AMD Radeon Settings → Display. You can create custom resolutions here.
5. **Registry fix**: If the resolution option is simply missing, check `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Video` for any overrides.
6. **Safe Mode test**: Boot into Safe Mode. If the correct resolution works there, it's a driver conflict in normal mode.
A user's profile is corrupted and they can't log in. They get a 'Temporary Profile' message.

A temporary profile means Windows can't load the user's normal profile. Their files are still on the disk.

**Fix the profile (registry method):**
1. Log in as a different admin account.
2. Open Registry Editor (`regedit`).
3. Navigate to: `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\ProfileList`
4. Look through the SID subkeys. Find the one for the affected user. There might be two entries:
   - One ending in `.bak` (the real profile)
   - One without `.bak` (the temporary profile)
5. Rename the one without `.bak` to `.bak2`.
6. Remove `.bak` from the real profile key.
7. Click the renamed key. Make sure 'RefCount' is 0 and 'State' is 0.
8. Restart and log in as the user.

**If that doesn't work — create a new profile and migrate data:**
1. Create a new local user account.
2. Log in as the new user (to create the profile).
3. Log out and back in as admin.
4. Copy the old user's files from `C:\Users\oldusername` to `C:\Users\newusername` (Desktop, Documents, Downloads, etc.).
5. Rename the new account to match the old username if needed.

**Prevention:** Enable roaming profiles or folder redirection in a domain environment to protect against profile corruption.
Should I upgrade from an HDD to an SSD? Is it worth it?

Yes, upgrading from an HDD to an SSD is the single biggest performance improvement you can make on an older computer.

**Speed difference:**
- HDD: ~100 MB/s read/write. Mechanical parts — a spinning disk with a moving arm.
- SATA SSD: ~550 MB/s. No moving parts. 5x faster.
- NVMe SSD: ~3,500 MB/s. Uses a different interface. 35x faster than HDD.

**What you'll notice:**
- Windows boot time: 2-3 minutes on HDD → 10-15 seconds on SSD.
- Programs open instantly instead of bouncing in the taskbar.
- File copies are much faster.
- The computer feels responsive even with multiple apps open.

**How to upgrade:**
1. Buy an SSD that fits your computer (2.5-inch SATA for most laptops, M.2 NVMe for newer ones).
2. Clone your existing drive: Use free software like Macrium Reflect or Samsung Data Migration (if you bought a Samsung SSD). This copies everything — Windows, programs, files — to the new SSD.
3. Swap the drives: Open the laptop, remove the HDD, insert the SSD.
4. Boot up. Everything should be exactly the same but faster.

**Tip:** 256 GB is the minimum for Windows + basic apps. 512 GB gives comfortable room. If you need lots of storage, keep the old HDD as a secondary drive for files and put the OS on the SSD.
Chrome is using a lot of memory and my computer slows down. Is this normal?

Chrome does use more RAM than other browsers, but there are ways to manage it.

1. Check what's using memory: Open Chrome and press Shift+Esc to open Chrome's Task Manager. This shows memory usage per tab and extension. Look for tabs or extensions using hundreds of MB.

2. Reduce open tabs: Each tab uses 50-300 MB of RAM. If you have 30 tabs open, that could be 3-9 GB. Close tabs you're not using, or use a tab suspender extension like 'The Great Suspender' to pause inactive tabs.

3. Disable unnecessary extensions: Go to chrome://extensions. Turn off extensions you rarely use. Some extensions run constantly in the background and eat memory.

4. Clear browsing data: Settings > Privacy and security > Clear browsing data. Clear cached images, cookies, and site data. A large cache can slow Chrome down.

5. Enable memory saver: Go to chrome://settings/performance. Turn on 'Memory Saver'. This automatically suspends tabs you haven't used in a while.

6. Consider switching to Edge: Microsoft Edge uses the same engine as Chrome but manages memory better on Windows. You can import all your bookmarks, passwords, and extensions.
How do you configure automatic Windows updates using Group Policy?

Configuring Windows Updates via GPO provides centralized control. Open Group Policy Management Console (gpmc.msc), create or edit a GPO linked to the appropriate OU. Navigate to Computer Configuration → Administrative Templates → Windows Components → Windows Update. Key settings: 'Configure Automatic Updates' — enable and choose option 4 (Auto download and schedule install). Set the install day (0=every day, 1=Sunday through 7=Saturday) and time. 'Specify intranet Microsoft update service location' — if using WSUS, enter the server URL (http://wsusserver:8530) for both the update and statistics server. 'Do not connect to any Windows Update Internet locations' — enable if you want updates exclusively from WSUS. 'Enable client-side targeting' — enable and specify the WSUS computer group name so computers automatically join the correct group. 'No auto-restart with logged on users for scheduled automatic updates installations' — consider enabling to prevent disruption during work hours. 'Automatic Updates detection frequency' — set how often clients check for updates (default 22 hours with random offset). For Windows 10/11 feature updates: 'Select when Preview Builds and Feature Updates are received' — set deferral days (e.g., 90 days for production). 'Select when Quality Updates are received' — defer quality updates (e.g., 7 days for production, 0 for pilot). After configuring, run 'gpupdate /force' on target machines and verify with 'gpresult /r'. Monitor compliance through WSUS reports.
Windows Search is not finding my files.

If Windows Search returns incomplete or no results:

1. **Rebuild the search index**: Settings → Privacy & Security → Searching Windows → Advanced indexing options → Advanced → Rebuild.
2. **Check indexed locations**: In the same Indexing Options window, click Modify and make sure your important folders are checked.
3. **Enable content indexing**: For the drive, right-click it → Properties → check 'Allow files on this drive to have contents indexed'.
4. **Restart Windows Search**: Run `services.msc`, find 'Windows Search', right-click → Restart.
5. **Reset Windows Search** (PowerShell admin):
   ```powershell
   Get-AppxPackage Microsoft.Windows.Search | Reset-AppxPackage
   ```
6. **Check file types**: By default, Search indexes content for common file types (.txt, .doc, .pdf) but only filenames for others. In Indexing Options → Advanced → File Types, add extensions and set to 'Index Properties and File Contents'.
7. **Alternative**: Use Everything by Voidtools — it's instant, lightweight, and indexes every file by filename. For content search, use Agent Ransack.
What is Kubernetes and what problems does it solve?

Kubernetes (K8s) is a container orchestration platform:

**The problem it solves**: Running containers at scale. Docker runs containers on one machine, but how do you:
- Run 100+ containers across multiple servers?
- Restart a container if it crashes?
- Scale up when traffic increases?
- Do rolling updates without downtime?
- Load balance between container replicas?

Kubernetes solves all of these.

**Key concepts**:
- **Cluster**: A set of machines (nodes) managed by Kubernetes.
- **Node**: A worker machine that runs containers.
- **Pod**: The smallest deployable unit — one or more containers that share network and storage.
- **Deployment**: Manages replicas of pods, handles rolling updates.
- **Service**: Provides a stable network endpoint to reach pods.
- **Namespace**: Logical isolation within a cluster.

**Basic commands**:
```bash
# Get cluster info
kubectl cluster-info
# List pods
kubectl get pods
kubectl get pods -A  # All namespaces
# Describe a pod
kubectl describe pod my-pod
# View logs
kubectl logs my-pod
kubectl logs my-pod -f  # Follow
# Shell into a pod
kubectl exec -it my-pod -- /bin/bash
# Apply a manifest
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
# Scale
kubectl scale deployment my-app --replicas=5
# Rolling update
kubectl set image deployment/my-app my-app=myapp:v2
```

**When to use Kubernetes**:
- Microservices architecture with many services.
- Need for auto-scaling and high availability.
- CI/CD with rolling deployments.
- Multi-cloud or hybrid cloud.

**When it's overkill**:
- Single application on a few servers.
- Small team without DevOps expertise.
- Simple deployment needs (use Docker Compose or a PaaS instead).

**Managed Kubernetes**: AKS (Azure), EKS (AWS), GKE (Google) — they manage the control plane, you manage the workloads.
How do I configure and manage BitLocker encryption in an enterprise environment?

BitLocker encrypts entire drives to protect data at rest. Enterprise deployment requires planning.

**Prerequisites**:
- TPM 2.0 (recommended) or TPM 1.2 for key storage.
- UEFI firmware with Secure Boot (recommended).
- Windows Pro, Enterprise, or Education.

**GPO Configuration** (Computer Configuration → Administrative Templates → Windows Components → BitLocker Drive Encryption):

1. **Operating System Drives**:
   - 'Require additional authentication at startup': configure TPM + PIN, TPM + USB, or TPM-only.
   - 'Choose how BitLocker-protected drives can be recovered': enable AD DS backup of recovery keys.
   - Encryption method: XTS-AES 256-bit (recommended for fixed drives).

2. **Recovery key storage**:
   - **Active Directory**: keys are stored as attributes on computer objects. Enable 'Store BitLocker recovery information in AD DS' and 'Do not enable BitLocker until recovery information is stored.'
   - **Azure AD/Entra ID**: keys auto-escrow for Azure AD joined devices.
   - **MBAM** (Microsoft BitLocker Administration and Monitoring): dedicated portal for key management and compliance reporting.

**Deployment**:
```powershell
# Enable BitLocker on C: with TPM protector
Enable-BitLocker -MountPoint "C:" -EncryptionMethod XtsAes256 -TpmProtector

# Add recovery password protector (backs up to AD)
Add-BitLockerKeyProtector -MountPoint "C:" -RecoveryPasswordProtector

# Check status
Get-BitLockerVolume | Select MountPoint, VolumeStatus, EncryptionPercentage, ProtectionStatus
```

**Intune deployment**: Device Configuration → Endpoint Protection → Windows Encryption. Configure encryption method, TPM settings, and recovery key escrow to Azure AD.

**Management tasks**:
- **Recovery**: if a user triggers recovery (BIOS change, TPM issue), find the recovery key in AD (BitLocker Recovery tab on the computer object) or Azure AD.
- **Suspend BitLocker** before BIOS updates or hardware changes: `Suspend-BitLocker -MountPoint "C:" -RebootCount 1`
- **Monitor compliance**: use MBAM reports or Intune compliance policies to ensure all devices are encrypted.
How do I set up a network monitoring solution using Zabbix?

Zabbix is a powerful open-source monitoring platform for networks, servers, and applications.

**1. Install Zabbix Server** (Ubuntu 22.04):
```bash
# Add repository
wget https://repo.zabbix.com/zabbix/6.4/ubuntu/pool/main/z/zabbix-release/zabbix-release_6.4-1+ubuntu22.04_all.deb
sudo dpkg -i zabbix-release_6.4-1+ubuntu22.04_all.deb
sudo apt update

# Install server, frontend, and agent
sudo apt install zabbix-server-mysql zabbix-frontend-php zabbix-apache-conf zabbix-sql-scripts zabbix-agent

# Set up the MySQL database
mysql -uroot -p
CREATE DATABASE zabbix CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_bin;
CREATE USER 'zabbix'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'password';
GRANT ALL ON zabbix.* TO 'zabbix'@'localhost';

# Import schema
zcat /usr/share/zabbix-sql-scripts/mysql/server.sql.gz | mysql -uzabbix -p zabbix

# Configure /etc/zabbix/zabbix_server.conf:
DBPassword=password

# Start services
sudo systemctl enable zabbix-server zabbix-agent apache2
sudo systemctl start zabbix-server zabbix-agent apache2
```

**2. Initial web setup**: access http://server/zabbix, complete the wizard, login with Admin/zabbix.

**3. Monitor hosts**:
- **Agent-based**: install Zabbix agent on each server. Collects CPU, memory, disk, network, and process metrics.
- **SNMP**: for network devices (switches, routers, firewalls, printers). Add SNMP interfaces.
- **ICMP/simple checks**: basic ping and port monitoring without agents.

**4. Templates**: apply built-in templates for common monitoring:
- 'Linux by Zabbix agent' – comprehensive Linux monitoring.
- 'Windows by Zabbix agent' – Windows server monitoring.
- 'Interfaces SNMP' – network device interfaces.

**5. Alerting**: Configure triggers (e.g., CPU > 80% for 10 minutes), then set up actions to send email, Slack, or PagerDuty notifications.

**6. Dashboards**: create custom dashboards showing network maps, server health, and problem lists.

**Best practices**: use auto-discovery to find new devices, implement host groups for organization, set up maintenance periods for planned outages, and archive old data with housekeeping settings.
What is Power Automate and how can IT use it?

Power Automate (formerly Microsoft Flow) is a workflow automation tool in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem:

**What it does**: Connects different services and automates workflows without code — e.g., 'When a new email arrives with an attachment, save it to SharePoint and notify me in Teams.'

**Common IT automation use cases**:
1. **Ticket management**: When a new email hits the support mailbox → create a ticket in ServiceNow/Jira → assign based on keywords → notify the team in Teams.
2. **Onboarding**: When a new user is added to AD → create their mailbox → assign licenses → send a welcome email with setup instructions.
3. **Approval workflows**: When someone requests admin access → send approval request to manager → if approved, add to security group → log the change.
4. **Monitoring**: When an Azure alert fires → create a Teams message → if critical, send SMS to on-call.
5. **File management**: When a file is uploaded to SharePoint → scan with Defender → move to appropriate folder → notify the uploader.

**Types of flows**:
- **Cloud flow**: Triggered by an event (email received, item created, schedule).
- **Desktop flow (RPA)**: Automates desktop applications (legacy apps without APIs). Uses UI recording.
- **Business process flow**: Guides users through a multi-step process.

**Key connectors**: Microsoft 365, SharePoint, Teams, Outlook, OneDrive, Azure AD, ServiceNow, Slack, SQL Server, HTTP (for custom APIs), and 500+ others.

**Example flow**:
```
Trigger: When a new email arrives (to: itsupport@company.com)
→ Condition: Subject contains 'urgent'
  → Yes: Post message to Teams 'Urgent Support' channel
  → No: Add to SharePoint 'Support Queue' list
→ Send reply: 'We received your request, ticket #XYZ'
```

**Licensing**: Basic connectors are included with Microsoft 365. Premium connectors (ServiceNow, Salesforce, SQL) require a Power Automate license (~$15/user/month).
What is Azure Storage and what are the different types?

Azure Storage is Microsoft's cloud storage service. There are four types, each for a different use case.

**1. Blob Storage (Binary Large Object):**
- For: Files, images, videos, backups, logs — any unstructured data.
- Think of it as: A cloud hard drive for files.
- Access tiers: Hot (frequent access, higher storage cost), Cool (infrequent, lower cost), Archive (rarely accessed, cheapest).
- Example: Storing backup files, serving images for a website.

**2. File Storage (Azure Files):**
- For: Shared file storage accessible via SMB protocol.
- Think of it as: A network drive in the cloud.
- You can mount it as a drive letter on Windows or mount it on Linux.
- Example: Replacing an on-premises file server. Map Z: to Azure Files.

**3. Table Storage:**
- For: Structured data without a full database.
- Think of it as: A simple NoSQL database.
- Good for: Configuration data, user profiles, device information.
- Not for: Complex queries — use Azure SQL or Cosmos DB for that.

**4. Queue Storage:**
- For: Storing messages between application components.
- Think of it as: A to-do list for your applications.
- Example: Web app puts a task in the queue, a background worker picks it up and processes it.

**How to access Azure Storage:**
- Azure Portal: portal.azure.com > Storage accounts
- Azure Storage Explorer: Free desktop app for browsing and managing storage.
- CLI: `az storage blob list --account-name myaccount --container-name mycontainer`
- SDKs: Python, C#, Java, JavaScript libraries available.
What is Group Policy and how do I use it?

Group Policy (GPO) is a Windows feature for centralized management of computer and user settings:

**Local Group Policy** (standalone PC, requires Pro/Enterprise):
1. Press Win+R → `gpedit.msc`.
2. Navigate the tree: Computer Configuration (affects the machine) and User Configuration (affects the logged-in user).
3. Each policy has three states: Not Configured, Enabled, Disabled.

**Common useful policies**:
- **Disable USB storage**: Computer Config → Administrative Templates → System → Removable Storage Access → 'All Removable Storage classes: Deny all access' → Enabled.
- **Password policy**: Computer Config → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Account Policies → Password Policy.
- **Disable Windows Store**: Computer Config → Administrative Templates → Windows Components → Store.
- **Map network drives**: User Config → Preferences → Windows Settings → Drive Maps.

**Domain Group Policy** (Active Directory):
- Created in Group Policy Management Console (GPMC): `gpmc.msc` on a domain controller.
- GPOs link to OUs, domains, or sites.
- Precedence: Local → Site → Domain → OU (last applied wins).
- Use `gpresult /r` on a client to see which policies are applied.
- Force update: `gpupdate /force`.

**Troubleshooting**:
- `gpresult /h report.html` — generates a detailed HTML report of all applied policies.
- Event Viewer → Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows → GroupPolicy → Operational.
What is Windows Sandbox and how is it useful for IT support?

Windows Sandbox is a lightweight, disposable virtual desktop environment built into Windows 10/11 Pro and Enterprise. Enable it: Settings → Apps → Optional Features → More Windows Features → Windows Sandbox. It creates an isolated Windows instance that starts clean every time—when you close it, everything inside is permanently deleted. IT support uses: 1) Testing suspicious email attachments or downloads in a safe environment. 2) Testing software installations before deploying to users. 3) Running potentially unstable applications without risking the host. 4) Testing GPO or registry changes safely. 5) Browsing untrusted websites. It requires: virtualization enabled in BIOS, 4GB+ RAM, 1GB free disk. It's faster than spinning up a full VM because it shares the host's kernel and dynamically generates a clean Windows image. Configuration files (.wsb) let you customize: shared folders, networking, startup scripts, and memory allocation.
How do I fix 'The instruction at 0x... referenced memory at 0x... The memory could not be read' errors on Windows?

This error indicates an application tried to access an invalid memory address. Steps: 1) Update the offending application to its latest version. 2) Update GPU drivers—graphics-intensive apps often trigger this. 3) Run 'sfc /scannow' and 'DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth' to repair system files. 4) Test RAM with Windows Memory Diagnostic (mdsched.exe) or MemTest86—faulty RAM is a common hardware cause. 5) Check if the error correlates with a specific DLL—if so, re-register it with 'regsvr32 <dll>'. 6) Disable DEP (Data Execution Prevention) for the specific application as a temporary workaround via System Properties → Performance Options → DEP tab, but only if the app vendor recommends it. If the error is system-wide and RAM tests pass, consider a clean Windows install.
How do I set up an Azure Virtual Network (VNet) with subnets and network security groups?

Azure networking fundamentals: 1) **Create the VNet**: Azure Portal → Virtual Networks → Create. Name it, choose a region, set the address space (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16). 2) **Add subnets**: During creation, add subnets: web-subnet (10.0.1.0/24), app-subnet (10.0.2.0/24), db-subnet (10.0.3.0/24). 3) **Network Security Groups (NSGs)**: Create an NSG for each subnet tier. NSG-Web: Allow inbound 80/443 from Internet, allow 22/3389 from your IP. NSG-App: Allow inbound app port from web-subnet only. NSG-DB: Allow inbound 1433/3306/5432 from app-subnet only. 4) **Associate NSGs**: Go to each subnet → Network Security Group → select the appropriate NSG. 5) **Key NSG rules**: Priority matters — lower number = higher priority. Default rules allow all outbound, allow intra-VNet, and deny all inbound (except intra-VNet and load balancer). 6) **NAT Gateway**: For outbound internet access from private subnets without public IPs, create a NAT Gateway and associate it with the subnet. 7) **Service Endpoints**: For secure access to Azure services (Storage, SQL Database), enable service endpoints on the subnet. This keeps traffic on the Azure backbone instead of going over the internet. 8) **VNet Peering**: To connect VNets (e.g., production to management), create a peering connection. Traffic stays on the Azure backbone.
How do I manage licenses and reduce costs in Microsoft 365?

Optimize your M365 licensing: 1) **Audit current usage** — in Microsoft 365 admin center → Reports → Usage. Check which services users actually use. A user with an E5 license who only uses email and Teams might only need E3 or Business Basic. 2) **Remove unused licenses** — go to Users → Active users, sort by 'Licenses' and look for users with licenses assigned but no recent activity. Use the 'Inactive users' report. 3) **Right-size licenses** — match license type to user needs: frontline workers get F1/F3, standard users get E3/Business Standard, power users and admins get E5. 4) **Shared mailboxes** — convert departed users' mailboxes to shared mailboxes, which don't require a license (up to 50GB). 5) **Group-based licensing** — use Azure AD groups to automatically assign and remove licenses based on department or role, preventing manual errors. 6) **Review add-ons** — check for duplicate capabilities (e.g., paying for a third-party meeting tool when Teams is included). 7) **Use the Licensing page** — admin center → Billing → Licenses shows how many licenses are assigned vs. purchased. Cancel excess.
How do I change the computer name in Windows?

Several ways to rename a PC:

1. **Settings**: Settings → System → About → 'Rename this PC' → enter new name → Restart.
2. **System Properties**: Win+R → `sysdm.cpl` → Computer Name tab → Change → enter new name → OK → Restart.
3. **Command line (admin)**:
   ```cmd
   :: View current name
   hostname
   :: Rename (requires restart)
   wmic computersystem where name="%computername%" call rename name="NEW-PC-NAME"
   ```
4. **PowerShell**:
   ```powershell

   ```

**Naming conventions** (best practices):

**After renaming**: Some apps may break if they reference the old name. Check: mapped drives using the old name, remote desktop shortcuts, any scripts with hardcoded computer names.
What are all the ways to take screenshots in Windows?

Windows offers several built-in screenshot methods:

1. **Print Screen (PrtScn)**: Captures the entire screen to clipboard. Paste with Ctrl+V in any app.
2. **Alt + Print Screen**: Captures only the active window to clipboard.
3. **Win + Print Screen**: Captures full screen and auto-saves to Pictures\Screenshots.
4. **Win + Shift + S** (Snipping Tool): Opens the snip toolbar — choose rectangular, freeform, window, or full-screen snip. The capture goes to clipboard and shows a notification to annotate/save.
5. **Snipping Tool app**: Search for 'Snipping Tool' in Start. Supports delayed screenshots (3, 5, or 10 seconds), recording screen video (Win11), and annotation.
6. **Win + G** (Game Bar): For capturing games. Press Win+Alt+PrtScn for a game screenshot, or Win+Alt+R to record video.

Third-party alternatives: ShareX (free, feature-rich), Greenshot, Lightshot.
How do I troubleshoot a VM that won't start in VMware vSphere?

VM startup failures in vSphere have several common causes:

**1. Check the error message**:
- Right-click the VM → Power On. The Tasks panel at the bottom shows the specific error.

**2. Common issues and fixes**:

**'File locked' or 'Cannot open the disk'**:
- Another host or process has a lock on the VMDK file.
- SSH into the ESXi host and check: `vmkfstools -D /vmfs/volumes/datastore/vmname/vmname.vmdk`
- If a stale lock exists after a host crash, the lock file (.lck) may need to be manually removed (only if the VM is truly not running anywhere).

**'Insufficient resources'**:
- The host doesn't have enough CPU or memory to power on the VM.
- Check host resource usage. Consider migrating other VMs or reducing this VM's reservation.
- If using admission control, it may block power-on to maintain HA guarantees.

**'Cannot find the virtual disk'**:
- The VMDK file was moved, deleted, or the datastore is inaccessible.
- Verify datastore connectivity: browse the datastore in the vSphere Client.
- If the file was deleted, restore from backup.

**'The virtual machine has an invalid configuration'**:
- Edit the VM settings and check for removed or misconfigured hardware (e.g., a CD-ROM pointing to a missing ISO, or a network adapter connected to a deleted port group).

**'Module Disk power on failed'**:
- Check if the VMDK is a thin-provisioned disk on a full datastore. Free space on the datastore.
- Verify VMDK descriptor file matches the flat file.

**3. Check VMware logs**:
- `/var/log/vmware/hostd.log` on the ESXi host.
- The VM's `vmware.log` in its folder on the datastore.

**4. General steps**:
- Try power on from a different host in the cluster.
- Remove and re-add the VM from inventory (don't delete from disk).
- Check host event logs for hardware errors (memory, storage controller).
How do I use System Restore to fix Windows?

System Restore rolls your computer back to an earlier point in time. It undoes system changes (driver installs, updates, registry changes) without affecting your personal files.

**How to use it:**
1. Search for 'Create a restore point' in Start.
2. In the System Properties window, click 'System Restore'.
3. Click Next. Choose a restore point from the list — pick one from before your problem started.
4. Click 'Scan for affected programs' to see what will be removed.
5. Click Next > Finish. The computer will restart and restore.

**If Windows won't boot:**
Force power off 3 times during boot to enter recovery. Troubleshoot > Advanced options > System Restore.

**Turn on System Restore (if it's off):**
1. Search for 'Create a restore point' > select your C: drive > click 'Configure'.
2. Select 'Turn on system protection'. Set the disk space to 5-10%.
3. Click OK.

**Create a manual restore point before making changes:**
Same window > click 'Create' > name it (e.g., 'Before driver update') > click Create.

**What System Restore does NOT restore:**
- Personal files (documents, photos, music) — these are not affected.
- Passwords — if you changed your password after the restore point, the old password won't come back.
- Malware — System Restore sometimes restores the malware too. Run a full scan after restoring.
How do I create a bootable USB drive for Windows installation?

Two main methods to create a Windows installation USB:

**Method 1: Microsoft Media Creation Tool** (recommended)
1. Go to microsoft.com/software-download/windows11 (or windows10).
2. Download the Media Creation Tool.
3. Run it → Accept license → 'Create installation media for another PC'.
4. Select language, edition, and architecture (64-bit).
5. Choose 'USB flash drive' → select your USB (8 GB+) → it will download and create the bootable USB.

**Method 2: Using an ISO with Rufus**

2. Download Rufus (rufus.ie) — free, portable, no install needed.

4. In Rufus: Device = your USB, Boot selection = the ISO file.

6. Click Start.

**For Linux ISOs**: Use Rufus, balenaEtcher, or Ventoy (Ventoy lets you put multiple ISOs on one USB and choose at boot).

**Boot from USB**:
1. Restart the PC.
2. Press the boot menu key (F12, Esc, or F2 depending on manufacturer).
3. Select the USB drive.
4. If it doesn't appear: Enter BIOS → disable Secure Boot → enable USB boot → reorder boot priority.

**Tip**: Use Ventoy if you need multiple tools on one USB — you can add Windows, Linux, rescue disks, and diagnostic tools all on one drive.
How do I optimize a slow SQL query?

SQL query optimization follows a systematic approach:

**1. Identify the slow query**:
- Enable slow query logging: MySQL (`slow_query_log = 1`, `long_query_time = 2`), PostgreSQL (`log_min_duration_statement = 2000`).
- Use your application's query profiler or APM tool.

**2. Analyze the execution plan**:
```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 123 AND status = 'pending';
```
Look for: full table scans (Seq Scan in PostgreSQL, ALL in MySQL), high estimated rows, sort operations on large datasets.

**3. Add appropriate indexes**:
```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_status ON orders(customer_id, status);
```
Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY, and GROUP BY. Composite indexes should match the query's column order.

**4. Common optimizations**:
- **Avoid SELECT *** – only retrieve needed columns. This reduces I/O and allows covering indexes.
- **Rewrite subqueries as JOINs** – correlated subqueries execute once per row; JOINs are usually more efficient.
- **Use LIMIT for large result sets** – pagination with LIMIT/OFFSET or keyset pagination.
- **Avoid functions on indexed columns** – `WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2024` can't use an index; use `WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2025-01-01'`.
- **Batch large operations** – UPDATE/DELETE millions of rows in chunks to avoid long locks.
- **Optimize JOINs** – ensure join columns are indexed and data types match.

**5. Database-level tuning**:
- Increase buffer pool / shared buffers to cache more data in memory.
- Update table statistics (`ANALYZE` in PostgreSQL, `ANALYZE TABLE` in MySQL).
- Consider partitioning for very large tables (by date range is common).

**6. Application-level improvements**:
- Cache frequently-read, rarely-changed data (Redis, Memcached).
- Use connection pooling (PgBouncer, ProxySQL).
- Implement read replicas for read-heavy workloads.
A Group Policy change I made isn't applying to a user's computer. How do I troubleshoot this?

Group Policy not applying is common and usually comes down to scope, filtering, or caching.

1. Force a Group Policy update: On the user's computer, open Command Prompt as admin and run:
```
gpupdate /force
```
This forces the computer to re-download policies from the domain controller right now.

2. Check what's actually applied: Run:
```
gpresult /r
```
This shows all applied GPOs for the computer and the user. Look for your GPO in the list. If it's not there, it's not applying.

3. Get the full report: Run:
```
gpresult /h C:\gpreport.html
```
Open the HTML file in a browser. It shows every GPO, whether it applied or was denied, and why.

4. Check the GPO scope: In Group Policy Management Console (GPMC), find your GPO. Check:
   - Is it linked to the right OU (Organizational Unit)? The user or computer must be in that OU.
   - Is the link enabled? (Right-click > check 'Link Enabled')
   - Is the GPO enabled? (Right-click GPO > GPO Status > should not be 'All settings disabled')

5. Check security filtering: By default GPOs apply to 'Authenticated Users'. If someone changed the filtering, the user or their group must be listed under Security Filtering.

6. Check for conflicting GPOs: A GPO linked at a higher level might override yours. GPOs apply in order: Local > Site > Domain > OU (last one wins).
How do I set up alerting so I'm notified when a critical service goes down?

Multi-channel alerting strategy: 1) **Choose what to monitor**: Critical services (DNS, DHCP, email, file shares, web apps, database), server health (CPU, memory, disk), network devices (switches, routers, firewalls, WAN links), certificate expiration, backup success/failure. 2) **Choose a monitoring tool**: PRTG (free up to 100 sensors, auto-discovers devices), Uptime Kuma (free, simple), Zabbix (free, powerful), Datadog/New Relic (SaaS, paid). 3) **Configure checks**: HTTP checks for web applications (check response code AND response time). TCP port checks for services. Ping/ICMP for device availability. SNMP for network device metrics. WMI/PowerShell for Windows-specific metrics. 4) **Alert thresholds**: Don't alert on momentary spikes — use sustained conditions (e.g., CPU > 90% for 5 minutes, not 1 second). Define Warning (yellow) and Critical (red) thresholds. 5) **Notification channels**: Email for all alerts. Slack/Teams webhook for the IT channel. SMS/phone call for critical after-hours alerts. PagerDuty/OpsGenie for on-call rotation and escalation. 6) **Escalation policy**: Alert the on-call person immediately. If not acknowledged in 15 minutes, alert the backup. If not acknowledged in 30 minutes, alert the IT manager. 7) **Reduce alert fatigue**: Tune thresholds to minimize false positives. Group related alerts (don't send 50 alerts when one switch dies — send one 'Switch X down, 50 devices affected'). Schedule maintenance windows to suppress alerts during planned work.
How do I manage Windows Update for Business?

Windows Update for Business (WUfB) uses cloud policies instead of WSUS for update management.
